doc_diff:
@@ -450,6 +450,9 @@ The general rules for the various types of input:
   the supported range of seconds to nanoseconds).
 - For integer input, the resolution used to interpret the integer value is used
   as the resulting resolution (or capped to the supported range of seconds to nanoseconds).
+  Note: this has been changed in pandas 3.1.0 to also default to microseconds for the
+  resulting resolution (or nanoseconds when the precision requires it). See
+  :ref:`whatsnew_310.api_breaking.datetimelike_unit_numeric` for more details.
 
 For example, the following would always have given nanosecond resolution previously,
 but now infer:

@@ -266,6 +266,53 @@ still raises ``ValueError`` for a ``fold=1`` (DST-ambiguous) timestamp
 Backwards incompatible API changes
 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 
+.. _whatsnew_310.api_breaking.datetimelike_unit_numeric:
+
+Datetime/timedelta resolution for numeric input
+^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+
+In pandas 3.0, the default ``unit`` when creating ``datetime64`` or
+``timedelta64`` data was changed from nanoseconds to microseconds for many
+cases (e.g. constructing from strings or stdlib ``datetime`` objects). But for
+numeric input, it was changed to take the resolution used to interpret the
+input value as the resulting resolution. See
+:ref:`whatsnew_300.api_breaking.datetime_resolution_inference` in the 3.0
+release notes for more details.
+
+This means that, for example, ``pd.to_timedelta([1], unit="s")`` now had ``s``
+resolution instead of ``ns``. An unintended side effect of this change is that
+doing arithmetic with such ``timedelta64[s]`` data, which preserves the ``s``
+resolution, could lead to unexpected (rounded) results (see :issue:`65608`).
+
+To ensure a more consistent use of resolution, construction with numeric input
+will now also default to microseconds (or nanoseconds if the precision of the
+input requires it).
+
+Specifically, :func:`to_datetime`, :func:`to_timedelta`, :class:`Timestamp`,
+and :class:`Timedelta` constructors will still use the ``unit`` argument to
+convert numeric input, but no longer use that resolution for the resulting
+``dtype``. For example, the following cases now all default to microseconds:
+
+.. code-block:: pycon
+
+   >>> print(pd.to_datetime([1, 2], unit="s").dtype)
+   datetime64[us]
+   >>> print(pd.to_timedelta([1, 2], unit="s").dtype)
+   timedelta64[us]
+   >>> pd.Timestamp(1, unit="s").unit
+   'us'
+   >>> pd.Timedelta(1, unit="s").unit
+   'us'
+
+Compared to the behaviour in pandas 2.x, this means that those cases now give
+microsecond resolution instead of nanoseconds. Except for the ``pd.Timestamp(1,
+unit="s")`` case, which already used the input ``unit`` before pandas 3.0,
+and thus now gives microsecond instead of second resolution.
+
+If you actually need the specific resolution from the input data, use the
+:meth:`~Timestamp.as_unit` (or :meth:`Series.dt.as_unit`) method after
+construction to convert to the desired resolution.
+

doc_diff:
@@ -282,6 +282,42 @@ yields another ``timedelta64[ns]`` dtypes Series.
    td * -1
    td * pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4])
 
+.. _timedeltas.unit_preserving_arithmetic:
+
+Multiplying or dividing by a number keeps the resolution (``unit``) of the
+timedelta operand. When the result is not a whole number of that unit, the
+fractional part is truncated toward zero, so a coarse resolution can silently
+lose precision:
+
+.. ipython:: python
+
+   td_s = pd.Timedelta(1, unit="s").as_unit("s")
+   td_s.unit
+   td_s / 2
+   td_s * 1.99
+
+   ser_s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="timedelta64[s]")
+   ser_s / 2
+
+Convert to a finer resolution with :meth:`Timedelta.as_unit` or
+:meth:`Series.dt.as_unit` before the operation when the fractional part matters,
+or use floor division (``//``) to make the rounding explicit:
+
+.. ipython:: python
+
+   td_s.as_unit("ms") / 2
+   ser_s.dt.as_unit("ms") / 2
+
+Addition and subtraction between timedelta-like or datetime-like operands with
+different resolutions return the finer of the two resolutions, so no precision
+is lost in those operations.
+
+.. ipython:: python
+
+   td_ms = pd.Timedelta(500, unit="ms").as_unit("ms")
+   td_s + td_ms
+   (td_s + td_ms).unit
+
 Rounded division (floor-division) of a ``timedelta64[ns]`` Series by a scalar
 ``Timedelta`` gives a series of integers.
